body.heading: The moon does not sleep
paragraphs: Many people think the moon only comes out at night. But the moon is in the daytime sky almost as often as the night sky — it is just harder to notice.
The moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight bounces off it, day and night alike.

body.heading: Where to look
paragraphs: On a clear morning or afternoon, ask your adult to help you search the blue sky. The daytime moon looks pale and white, like a ghost of the night moon.
It is easiest to spot a few days before or after the full moon, when it is big and bright. Look low in the east in the morning and in the west in the afternoon.

body.heading: Keep a spotting diary
paragraphs: Every time you spot the daytime moon, draw its shape and write the date. Is it a round moon, a half moon, or a thin curved sliver?
Soon you will start noticing it everywhere. The moon was there all along, waiting for someone to look up.

takeaway: The moon is in the daytime sky very often — you just have to remember to look for it.
safetyNotes: Never look at the Sun while sky watching. Look only where your adult points, away from the sun.
